title: Economic Evaluation of Community-based Falls Prevention Interventions: a Systematic Methodological Overview of Systematic Reviews

subsections.section_title: Objectives and Scope of the Overview
subsections.content:
This overview is framed as a systematic review of systematic reviews and follows established reporting guidance to maximise transparency, reproducibility, and interpretability. In particular, the review process, study selection logic, and synthesis structure are aligned with PRISMA principles, which were developed to improve the completeness of reporting in systematic reviews and meta-analyses and to make key methodological decisions explicit for readers and decision-makers ref [1]. For an overview design, this emphasis on reporting is especially important because conclusions depend not only on the primary economic evaluations but also on how earlier reviews identified, appraised, and synthesised that evidence.

The review boundaries are intentionally narrow. It focuses on community-based falls prevention interventions for older adults and on reviews that include an economic component, such as cost-effectiveness, cost-utility, cost-benefit, or broader resource-use assessments. Hospital-only, residential long-term care, or purely clinical effectiveness reviews without economic evaluation are outside scope unless they directly inform community public health delivery. This delimitation is methodologically necessary because intervention setting, comparator structure, time horizon, and payer perspective strongly shape economic results; combining fundamentally different delivery contexts would reduce the interpretability of any cross-review methodological overview ref [1].

A further reporting boundary concerns what is being synthesised. The purpose of this overview is not to re-estimate pooled cost-effectiveness, but to map and critically compare the methods used across systematic reviews: search strategies, inclusion criteria for economic studies, quality appraisal tools, modelling assumptions, treatment of uncertainty, and handling of transferability across jurisdictions. Accordingly, the unit of analysis is the systematic review rather than the individual trial or model, while noting where review-level reporting obscures important features of the underlying economic evidence ref [1].

subsections.section_title: Objectives and Scope of the Overview
subsections.subsection_title: Conceptual Scope of Public Health Economic Models
subsections.content:
The economic evaluation of community-based falls prevention sits within the broader domain of public health modeling, where intervention effects are rarely confined to a single clinical pathway. Public health models must therefore represent interactions between individual risk, behavior, service uptake, and wider social and environmental determinants, rather than relying solely on narrowly specified disease-process frameworks. Squires et al. argue that model structure in public health should be grounded in a systems perspective, developed through explicit problem formulation, stakeholder engagement, and systematic consideration of determinants of health; these principles are directly relevant to falls prevention, where outcomes depend on mobility, housing conditions, adherence, comorbidity, and care pathways ref [2].

For this overview, the conceptual scope of eligible economic models is accordingly defined broadly. We consider models that evaluate not only fracture or hospital avoidance, but also downstream consequences for functional decline, long-term care use, quality of life, and resource use across health and social care sectors. This broader framing is consistent with guidance that public health interventions often generate diffuse, intersectoral, and time-dependent effects that are poorly captured by overly simple model structures ref [2], ref [2]. In practice, this implies attention to whether reviews included decision trees, Markov models, individual-level simulation, or other approaches capable of representing recurrence, heterogeneity, and complex causal pathways ref [2], ref [3].

A further implication is that model adequacy should be judged conceptually as well as technically. In falls prevention, structurally credible models should justify the choice of time horizon, recurrence assumptions, risk stratification, and handling of competing events such as institutionalization or death. They should also clarify whether the intervention is modeled as a one-off risk reduction or as part of a dynamic prevention system with changing adherence and exposure over time. This overview therefore treats model scope as a central methodological issue, because structural simplification can materially affect estimated cost-effectiveness and the transferability of findings to community public health decision-making ref [2], ref [3], ref [4].

subsections.section_title: Objectives and Scope of the Overview
subsections.content:
Equity is an important, but often under-specified, consideration in the economic evaluation of community-based falls prevention. Standard cost-effectiveness analyses typically adopt the implicit assumption that health gains are valued equally regardless of who benefits, yet this “a QALY is a QALY” position may be inadequate for public health interventions that differentially affect socially disadvantaged groups, older adults with frailty, or those facing barriers to service access ref [1]. In this overview, equity is therefore treated as a methodological feature of interest rather than as a peripheral ethical add-on.

Specifically, we consider whether included reviews and the primary economic evaluations they summarize examined distributional consequences across relevant population subgroups, such as age, sex, socioeconomic status, ethnicity, rurality, baseline fall risk, functional limitation, and living arrangement. We also note whether studies addressed differential uptake, adherence, or intervention reach, since these mechanisms can materially influence both efficiency and equity in prevention programmes. Where reported, we distinguish between simple subgroup analysis and more explicit equity-oriented approaches, including equity weighting, distributional analysis, or discussion of trade-offs between total health gain and reduction in unfair health inequalities ref [1].

Given the focus on community settings, equity considerations are especially salient because intervention effectiveness and resource use may depend on transportation, caregiver support, housing conditions, digital access, and local service capacity. Accordingly, this overview does not attempt to resolve normative debates about the appropriate social value of reducing inequalities; rather, it documents the extent to which equity-relevant assumptions, data, and outcomes were made visible in the review evidence base, and highlights where future falls prevention models could move beyond average-effect estimates toward more distribution-sensitive public health appraisal ref [1].

Methodological reviews of economic evaluations in community-based falls prevention should be framed as systematic reviews of review-level and study-level evidence, with prespecified objectives, eligibility criteria, search strategies, and data extraction procedures. Transparent reporting is essential because the interpretability of conclusions about modelling choices, costing approaches, and outcome valuation depends heavily on how reviews identify, select, and appraise the underlying literature. The PRISMA statement provides the core reporting framework for documenting review rationale, information sources, study selection, and synthesis methods, thereby improving reproducibility and critical appraisal ref [1].

In practice, review design should follow established systematic review methods, including protocol development, duplicate screening where feasible, explicit management of overlap between included reviews, and clear justification for any restrictions by language, date, or publication type. The Cochrane Handbook remains particularly relevant for structuring these processes, as it emphasises rigorous question formulation, comprehensive searching, standardised study selection, and transparent handling of bias and heterogeneity in evidence synthesis ref [3]. For methodological overviews in health economics, these principles are especially important because variation in perspective, time horizon, analytic approach, and model assumptions can generate substantial between-study heterogeneity even when interventions appear clinically similar.

Reporting should therefore move beyond a simple PRISMA flow diagram to include explicit descriptions of how economic evidence was classified and compared across reviews and primary studies. Useful reporting items include the decision rules for identifying full economic evaluations, the extraction framework for model-based versus trial-based analyses, and the methods used to summarise quality appraisal findings. Such detail supports a more robust interpretation of whether differences in reported cost-effectiveness reflect genuine intervention effects or merely divergent methodological choices ref [1], ref [3].

Economic model structure development is a pivotal methodological issue in reviews of community-based falls prevention because these interventions operate through multiple pathways, often extending beyond narrowly defined healthcare effects. The public health modelling literature argues that model structure should be grounded in an explicit conceptualisation of the decision problem rather than selected opportunistically from familiar clinical templates. In this view, structural development should begin with a documented understanding of the intervention, target population, causal mechanisms, contextual influences, and relevant outcomes, with transparency about why particular states, pathways, and feedbacks are included or omitted ref [2], ref [4].

For falls prevention, this implies that model structures should be capable of representing heterogeneity in baseline risk, recurrent falls, injury severity, fear of falling, functional decline, institutionalisation, and mortality, while also capturing consequences outside the healthcare sector when relevant. Squires et al. emphasize that public health models frequently need to accommodate complexity, multicomponent interventions, behavioural responses, and social determinants of health; overly simplified structures may therefore compromise validity and policy relevance ref [4]. Their framework further recommends a systems-oriented approach, iterative stakeholder engagement, and explicit justification of structural assumptions throughout model development ref [2].

In a methodological overview of systematic reviews, appraisal of model structure should therefore examine whether included economic evaluations reported a clear conceptual model, justified the choice of modelling technique, aligned time horizon and outcomes with intervention mechanisms, and considered broader public health impacts where appropriate. Particular attention should be paid to whether falls prevention models moved beyond short-term event counting toward representations of recurrent risk and longer-term trajectories, since these structural decisions materially influence estimated cost-effectiveness and transferability across community settings ref [2], ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Methodological Challenges in Public Health Economic Modeling
subsections.content:
Economic modeling of community-based falls prevention sits within the broader methodological difficulties of public health evaluation, where interventions are embedded in complex, adaptive systems rather than isolated clinical pathways. A recurring concern is that conventional decision-analytic structures can be too narrow to capture feedback loops, multicomponent delivery, intersectoral consequences, and heterogeneous effects across populations. Reviews of public health modeling therefore emphasize three particularly important challenges: incorporating non-healthcare costs and outcomes, addressing equity, and representing dynamic complexity and behavior change in a credible model structure ref [5].

These challenges are especially salient for older-population interventions. In health promotion for older adults, applied economic evaluations have often inadequately measured informal care, productivity and volunteer contributions, unrelated future costs in added life years, and broader capability or social participation benefits. Huter et al. show that only a small share of studies include such categories, and methods remain highly inconsistent, limiting comparability and potentially undervaluing interventions targeted at later life ref [2]. For falls prevention, this implies that models restricted to health-service utilization and health-related quality of life may miss substantial family, social care, and independence-related consequences.

Methodological guidance increasingly recommends a more explicit conceptual modeling phase before formal model construction. Squires et al. propose that good public health modeling should adopt a systems perspective, document the problem in detail, engage stakeholders throughout model development, and systematically consider the social determinants of health when defining causal pathways and outcomes ref [4]. For systematic reviews of economic evaluations in falls prevention, these principles suggest that methodological appraisal should extend beyond reporting quality to whether studies justified their model scope, perspective, time horizon, and handling of complexity in ways appropriate to community-based public health decision making ref [4], ref [5], ref [2].

subsections.subsection_title: Evidence from Economic Evaluations of Health Promotion for Older Adults
subsections.content:
Economic evidence on health promotion for older adults remains relatively limited and unevenly distributed across intervention types. A key systematic review of full economic evaluations for populations aged 65 years and older identified only 29 eligible studies from 2000–2015, with a strong concentration on fall prevention and far fewer evaluations of broader health promotion domains such as vaccination, nutrition, or multi-component community programmes ref [6]. This pattern suggests that the available evidence base is shaped as much by research priorities as by the underlying burden of preventable morbidity in later life.

Within that literature, the most consistent positive findings concern physical activity-based interventions, particularly those designed to maintain mobility, balance, and functional independence. The review by Dubas-Jakóbczyk et al. concluded that diverse fall-prevention exercise programmes frequently appeared cost-effective, although results depended on study quality, comparator choice, and the time horizon used to capture downstream benefits ref [6]. These findings are broadly aligned with wider evidence that preventive interventions for older adults can generate favorable cost-effectiveness profiles when they avert costly events such as fractures, hospitalization, and long-term care admission, but that transferability across settings is often limited by differences in service organization and baseline risk.

Methodologically, the older-adult health promotion literature highlights recurrent weaknesses that are directly relevant for community-based falls prevention research. Evaluations often rely on short follow-up periods, narrow health-sector perspectives, and limited measurement of non-health outcomes such as independence, social participation, or caregiver effects ref [6]. As a result, existing studies may underestimate the full value of upstream prevention in ageing populations. For this survey, the broader lesson is that evidence from health promotion for older adults supports the economic promise of prevention, but also underscores the need for longer-term, societally informed models capable of capturing heterogeneous trajectories of ageing and functional decline ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Empirical Evidence from Fall and Injury Prevention Interventions
subsections.content:
Empirical economic evidence on community-based fall and injury prevention suggests that both targeted exercise and broader safety-promotion strategies can generate meaningful health gains, although the strength of inference varies by design. In a randomized trial in New Zealand, a nurse-delivered home exercise programme for adults aged 75 years and older reduced falls by 46% and eliminated fall-related hospital admissions observed in the control group over one year, indicating that relatively low-intensity delivery models can retain effectiveness outside specialist services ref [2].

The same trial also reported favorable economic results: the programme cost NZ$1803 per fall prevented from the programme perspective, falling to NZ$155 per fall prevented when hospital costs averted were incorporated, with greater cost-effectiveness among participants aged 80 years and over ref [2]. This age-gradient is important for modeling because it implies that intervention value is highly sensitive to baseline risk, injury severity, and downstream healthcare utilization rather than intervention cost alone.

Complementing this individual-level evidence, a Swedish quasi-experimental evaluation of a five-year community elderly safety-promotion programme found that a multicomponent strategy combining environmental modifications with individually oriented measures could avert hip fractures and appear cost-effective when compared with the substantial treatment costs and quality-of-life losses associated with fracture events ref [7]. Taken together, these studies suggest that economic returns are most plausible when interventions either target high-risk older adults or prevent severe outcomes such as hip fracture and hospitalization; however, the evidence base remains methodologically heterogeneous, with results shaped by differences in outcome choice, analytic perspective, and the robustness of effectiveness estimation ref [7], ref [2].

subsections.subsection_title: Frameworks for Interpreting Public Health Economic Models
subsections.content:
Interpretation of economic models for community-based falls prevention should be guided by frameworks developed specifically for public health, rather than by clinical modelling conventions alone. Public health interventions often act through multiple pathways, interact with local service systems, and generate effects beyond healthcare use; consequently, overly simplified models risk misrepresenting both costs and value. Squires et al. argue that model interpretation should therefore begin from a systems perspective, with explicit attention to the intervention context, causal mechanisms, stakeholder perspectives, and the broader determinants of health that may mediate fall risk and downstream outcomes ref [2].

The methodological literature further identifies three recurrent interpretive challenges that are especially relevant to falls prevention reviews: capturing non-healthcare costs and outcomes, addressing equity implications, and representing complex, multi-component interventions within dynamic systems ref [4]. For example, exercise, home hazard modification, medication review, and multifactorial programmes may have heterogeneous uptake, adherence, and spillover effects across subgroups of older adults. Interpreting model results thus requires scrutiny of structural assumptions about behaviour, social interaction, and service delivery, not merely parameter uncertainty ref [4].

A useful appraisal lens is the four-phase conceptual modelling framework proposed by Squires et al., which links model development to the decision problem, stakeholder identification, problem conceptualisation, and formal justification of model structure ref [2]. Applied to falls prevention, this framework encourages reviewers to ask whether models adequately reflect community implementation pathways, long-term consequences, and distributional effects across frail, socially disadvantaged, or recurrent-faller populations. Such a framework does not eliminate uncertainty, but it improves transparency and helps distinguish between robust policy-relevant simplifications and structural omissions that may bias decision-making ref [2], ref [4].

subsections.subsection_title: Critical Appraisal Standards and Evidence Synthesis
subsections.content:
Critical appraisal in reviews of economic evidence for community-based falls prevention should distinguish between assessment of review conduct, appraisal of underlying trial quality, and appraisal of the economic methods themselves. The Cochrane Handbook provides the core standards for review design, study selection, risk-of-bias assessment, and synthesis of intervention effects, and remains the main benchmark for transparent evidence assembly in health intervention reviews ref [1]. For the reporting of the review process, PRISMA improves reproducibility by clarifying search strategies, eligibility decisions, and handling of heterogeneity across studies ref [2].

Economic components require additional scrutiny beyond conventional effectiveness appraisal. In falls prevention, studies often vary in time horizon, costing perspective, outcome metric, treatment of recurrent falls, and whether downstream consequences such as fractures, institutionalization, and quality-of-life change are incorporated. Consensus-based checklists such as CHEERS 2022 are useful for judging completeness of reporting in trial-based and model-based evaluations, while the Drummond criteria remain widely used to assess whether resource use, comparators, discounting, uncertainty, and incremental analysis are handled appropriately ref [3], ref [4]. When decision models are included, ISPOR-SMDM guidance is particularly relevant for evaluating structural assumptions, validation, and sensitivity analysis ref [5].

Evidence synthesis in this field is therefore rarely a simple meta-analysis of cost-effectiveness ratios. Instead, robust overviews typically use narrative or structured tabulation to compare intervention type, target population, setting, analytical perspective, and decision context, while separating transferability issues from internal validity. This is especially important for community falls prevention, where multi-component interventions and local service configurations generate substantial methodological heterogeneity and limit direct pooling of economic conclusions ref [1], ref [4].

For community-based falls prevention, implementation is not an operational afterthought but part of the economic decision itself. Reviews that report favorable incremental cost-effectiveness often abstract from imperfect uptake, variable adherence, and delivery capacity, yet these factors determine whether modeled value is realized in practice. A useful distinction is between the value of the intervention under current implementation and the additional value obtainable from improving implementation; this separates the question of whether a falls programme is efficient in principle from whether investing in dissemination, training, referral pathways, or adherence support is worthwhile [1].

This perspective also implies that decisions about programme content and implementation strategy should ideally be made jointly rather than sequentially. As argued in decision-analytic work on clinical practice change, an integral approach can alter the preferred option because implementation costs and effects may differ materially across alternatives [2]. In falls prevention, this is highly relevant when comparing home-based exercise, multifactorial assessment, or group programmes, whose effectiveness depends on different workforce models, participant engagement, and local service configuration. Systematic reviews should therefore interpret economic findings in light of implementation assumptions, scalability, and the decision context, not only trial-based ICERs.

Value assessment in this area should further extend beyond conventional cost-effectiveness thresholds. Priority-setting guidance emphasizes equity-relevant criteria not captured by standard CEA, including socioeconomic disadvantage, area of residence, severity or vulnerability, and wider non-health consequences [3]. For older populations at risk of falls, these considerations intersect with concerns about access, independence, caregiver burden, and distributional effects. Accordingly, decision makers should read review findings as one input into a broader deliberative process that combines efficiency, implementability, uncertainty, and equity when allocating resources to falls prevention services [1][3].

subsections.subsection_title: Limitations and Heterogeneity in Fall Prevention Evidence
subsections.content:
A persistent limitation in the fall-prevention evidence base is substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity across trials. Interventions grouped under common labels—such as “multifactorial,” “multiple component,” or “exercise”—often differ markedly in content, intensity, targeting, adherence support, and delivery setting, making pooled estimates difficult to interpret for economic purposes. This problem is especially salient in the long-running debate over whether single interventions should be preferred to more complex multifactorial strategies, since apparent differences in effectiveness may reflect variation in implementation and participant uptake rather than intervention class alone ref [12], ref [13].

Systematic review evidence confirms this heterogeneity. The Cochrane review of community-based multifactorial and multiple component interventions found variability in effects across outcomes and studies, with uncertainty arising from differences in baseline fall risk, assessment procedures, combinations of treatment components, and follow-up periods ref [4]. Related commentaries have similarly noted that multifactorial programmes may not consistently outperform well-designed single interventions such as exercise, particularly when adherence is high and the target population is clearly defined ref [12], ref [13]. For economic evaluation, this undermines transferability: cost-effectiveness estimates are highly sensitive to assumptions about who is reached, which components are actually delivered, and whether benefits accrue through reduced fall rates, fewer recurrent falls, or avoided injuries.

A further limitation is that many reviews synthesize effectiveness evidence from studies not designed with economic endpoints in mind. As a result, downstream models frequently rely on sparse fracture, hospitalisation, quality-of-life, and long-term care data, while also needing to extrapolate beyond trial horizons. In this context, heterogeneity should not be treated merely as statistical noise; it is a structural feature of community fall prevention that warrants subgroup analysis, transparent scenario testing, and cautious interpretation of summary cost-effectiveness claims ref [4].

For evidence synthesis, the main implication is that future reviews of economic evaluations in community-based falls prevention should move beyond simple narrative aggregation and adopt protocol-driven methods that explicitly align intervention, comparator, perspective, time horizon, and outcome domains. Standard systematic review guidance remains directly relevant here: review questions, eligibility criteria, and synthesis plans should be prespecified, and heterogeneity should be examined at both the clinical and methodological levels rather than treated as residual noise ref [3]. In this field, variation in intervention intensity, target risk group, costing methods, and effectiveness metrics frequently makes pooled conclusions about cost-effectiveness more uncertain than pooled conclusions about clinical efficacy.

A more informative synthesis strategy would therefore combine structured tabulation with conceptual grouping of studies by intervention logic and analytic design. Reviews should distinguish trial-based from model-based evaluations, separate single-component from multifactorial programmes, and report how resource use, fall-related outcomes, health-related quality of life, and downstream consequences such as institutionalisation are linked within each study. This is especially important in public health prevention, where model structure, assumptions about long-term benefit, and treatment of implementation can materially alter conclusions about value for money. Transparent handling of these elements would improve cross-study comparability and help decision-makers judge transferability across settings ref [3].

Finally, evidence syntheses should place greater emphasis on reporting uncertainty, applicability, and decision relevance. Rather than asking only whether an intervention is cost-effective, reviews should identify which parameters drive uncertainty, where evidence is sparse, and which populations or service configurations remain underrepresented. Such an approach would support a transition from descriptive review toward decision-oriented synthesis, clarifying where updated modelling, head-to-head economic comparison, and better reporting standards are most needed for community falls prevention policy ref [3].

Overall, the methodological overview suggests that evidence on the cost-effectiveness of community-based falls prevention is promising but remains difficult to synthesize into clear policy guidance because review-level conclusions are shaped by heterogeneous interventions, short analytic horizons, and inconsistent treatment of downstream outcomes beyond falls alone. Earlier reviews of economic evidence in health promotion for older people already highlighted recurrent weaknesses in perspective, outcome valuation, and transferability, and these concerns remain salient for falls prevention specifically ref [6], ref [5]. As a result, conclusions about “best buys” should be interpreted as contingent on modelling choices, implementation context, and the extent to which broader consequences such as independence, quality of life, and service utilization are captured.

Future work should move beyond asking whether falls prevention is cost-effective on average and instead examine which intervention packages are efficient for which populations and delivery systems. This implies greater use of decision-analytic models that reflect the complexity of public health pathways and explicitly justify structural assumptions ref [2], ref [4]. More consistent incorporation of equity considerations is also needed, since targeting strategies based solely on average cost-effectiveness may overlook distributional consequences across age, frailty, deprivation, or access barriers ref [10]. In parallel, the growing evidence base for multifactorial and multiple-component interventions indicates that future syntheses should better separate intervention content, implementation intensity, and adherence effects when comparing economic results ref [13].

In conclusion, the next generation of systematic reviews should combine stronger economic-methods appraisal with clearer reporting of decision context, model structure, and uncertainty, while primary studies should generate longer-term and implementation-relevant data. Such advances would make the evidence base more cumulative, more comparable across jurisdictions, and more useful for commissioners deciding how to scale community falls prevention.
